docs.title: Systems Platform and Intelligence Lab
docs.text: This site documents the sprc compute cluster: how to log in, how to run jobs, what is changing during the move to SLURM, and where to get help.

docs.title: What is changing
docs.text:
In June 2026 the cluster is moving to SLURM, the scheduler used by most university HPC systems. The change rolls out in stages so that you can adapt gradually.

SLURM is optional until June 30, which means your current direct-SSH workflow keeps working while you try the new commands. Soft enforcement begins on July 1: from that date, work you run inside an allocation gains time limits, fair-share scheduling, and GPU isolation, and batch submission with sbatch becomes available. A later date, announced ahead of time, brings hard enforcement, after which an allocation is required to use a compute node. The About the transition page explains the reasoning and the full timeline.

Migrate your data by Tuesday, June 30

The per-node home directories and the /mnt/data1 data drive on the compute nodes (sprc00 through sprc03) will be erased after June 30. Copy anything you want to keep to the shared storage before then, and mark your name in the migration sheet posted in #server. The Migrate your data page lists the steps.

docs.title: The one workflow change
docs.text:
Before you use a compute node, you request the resources you need with a single command. After that, you work the same way you do today, with the same code, conda environments, containers, VS Code Remote-SSH, and tmux.

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00     # request one GPU for four hours
squeue --me                            # see which node you were assigned
ssh <node>                             # connect and work as usual

Work that does not need a GPU follows the same path. You request CPU cores and memory and leave off --gres:

salloc --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=4:00:00

The Running jobs page covers allocations, long runs, batch jobs, and deadlines in full.

docs.title: See what is free
docs.text:
The live cluster status dashboard shows free GPUs, queue depth, and current contention. From a shell, three commands give you the same picture:

sinfo            # node and partition state: idle, mixed, or fully allocated
squeue           # everything queued and running across the cluster
squeue --me      # only your jobs

docs.title: The cluster at a glance
docs.text:
The cluster has four compute nodes, sprc00 through sprc03, each with two NVIDIA H100 NVL GPUs, for eight GPUs in total. You log in to a single login node at sprlab005.csl.illinois.edu, where your files live and from which you request compute.

Two partitions share that hardware. The default partition, main, accepts jobs of up to three days and handles all normal work. The debug partition is for short tests of up to one hour and gives quick turnaround. Select a partition with --partition (for example, --partition=debug). If you leave it off, your job runs in main.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
Ask in #server. If you are unsure how to move your current workflow onto SLURM, describe it in the channel and the sysadmin team will help you adapt it.

Maintained by the sysadmin team. Last updated 2026-06-25.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
A brief lookup for day-to-day use. The Running jobs page explains these in context.

Migrate your data by June 30

The per-node home directories and /mnt/data1 are erased after June 30. Move your data to shared storage first.

docs.title: Request a node
docs.text:
Request a GPU and a time limit, then connect to the node you are given:

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00            # 1 GPU for 4 hours, default partition (main)
salloc --gres=gpu:2 --time=2:00:00            # both GPUs on a node
salloc --gres=gpu:1 -p debug --time=0:30:00   # quick test on the debug partition

For CPU-only work, request cores and memory and leave off --gres:

salloc --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=4:00:00

After salloc returns, connect to the assigned node and work normally:

ssh <node>        # for example, sprc01
nvidia-smi        # the GPUs available to you

docs.title: Long runs
docs.text:
Keep an interactive long run alive in tmux so it survives a dropped connection:

tmux                                   # start tmux on the login node
salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=24:00:00    # hold the allocation
ssh <node>                             # detach with Ctrl-b d, reattach with tmux attach

docs.title: Submit a batch job
docs.text:
Batch submission becomes available at soft enforcement on July 1, once the June 30 storage migration is complete. Until then, use salloc in tmux for long runs.

sbatch --gres=gpu:1 --time=12:00:00 train.sh   # queue a job, then walk away
squeue --me                                    # watch it

A batch script sets its own options with #SBATCH lines:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --job-name=train
srun python train.py

docs.title: Watch your jobs
docs.text:
squeue --me                 # your queued and running jobs
squeue                      # everyone's jobs
squeue --me --start         # estimated start time for pending jobs
scontrol show job <jobid>   # full detail on one job

In the ST column, R means running and PD means pending. For a pending job, the NODELIST(REASON) column gives the reason: Resources means the GPUs you asked for are busy, and Priority means other jobs are ahead of you.

docs.title: See what is free
docs.text:
sinfo                       # partitions and node states
sinfo -N -l                 # one line per node, with detail

A node state of idle is free, mix is partly used, and alloc is fully allocated.

docs.title: Stop a job
docs.text:
scancel <jobid>             # cancel one job
scancel --me                # cancel all of your jobs

docs.title: After a job ends
docs.text:
sacct -j <jobid>                                   # what happened to a job
sacct -u <you> --starttime 2026-06-01              # your job history
sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqTRES

Values in the State column worth knowing:

State Meaning COMPLETED Finished cleanly (exit 0). TIMEOUT Reached the --time limit. Request more time on the next run. FAILED The program exited with a non-zero status. OUT_OF_MEMORY Used more memory than requested. Raise --mem or use less. CANCELLED Stopped by scancel, by you or by an admin.

docs.title: Common options
docs.text: Option Purpose --gres=gpu:1 Request 1 GPU (use :2 for both on a node). --time=HH:MM:SS Wall-clock limit. --partition=<name> (-p) Choose a partition. The default is main. --cpus-per-task=N (-c) Request N CPU cores. --mem=32G Request memory. --qos=expedite Use a granted deadline-priority window (ask in #server). --job-name=<name> (-J) Label your job.

docs.title: Partitions
docs.text: Partition Maximum time Use it for main (default) 3 days All normal work. debug 1 hour Short tests with quick turnaround.

docs.title: Need help?
docs.text: Ask in #server. If you are on a deadline, ask there about a priority window.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Short answers to common questions. If you are still stuck, ask in #server.

docs.title: My job was killed. Why?
docs.text:
Run sacct -j <jobid> and read the State column.

  • TIMEOUT means you reached the --time limit. Request more time on the next run, up to three days in main.
  • OUT_OF_MEMORY means the job used more memory than it requested. Add --mem=64G, or whatever you need, or reduce the batch size.
  • FAILED means your program exited with an error. Check its output log.
  • CANCELLED means someone ran scancel. If it was not you, an admin may have cancelled it, which is rare and always explained.

docs.title: Do I still have to do this? I used to just SSH in.
docs.text: SLURM is optional until June 30, and direct SSH continues to work through soft enforcement on July 1, so you can keep your current workflow for now. What begins on July 1 is that work you run inside an allocation gains time limits, fair-share scheduling, and, for GPU jobs, GPU isolation. At hard enforcement, on a date announced ahead of time, an allocation becomes required to use a compute node. Trying the new workflow now, while both still work, means no surprises later. See About the transition.

docs.title: I only need CPU, not a GPU. Does this apply to me?
docs.text:
Yes. SLURM schedules the whole compute node, not only its GPUs, so CPU-only work follows the same path. Leave off --gres and request cores and memory instead:

salloc --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=4:00:00

You still receive a time limit and the same fair-share scheduling, and at hard enforcement you still need an allocation to use a node. The only GPU-specific piece is GPU isolation, which has nothing to apply to a job that requested no GPU.

docs.title: What is the June 30 deadline about? Do I need to move my data?
docs.text: Yes, by Tuesday, June 30. The per-node home directories and the /mnt/data1 data drive on the compute nodes are erased after June 30, ahead of soft enforcement on July 1. Copy anything you want to keep to the shared storage, then mark your name in the migration sheet. The full steps are on the Migrate your data page. Shared storage has a 50 GB quota per user; if you need more, ask in #server.

docs.title: How do I ask for more than one GPU?
docs.text: --gres=gpu:2 gives you both GPUs on a node. Each node has two GPUs, so two is the maximum on a single node. Multi-node GPU jobs are possible but uncommon here, so ask if you need one.

docs.title: How do I know what is free before I ask?
docs.text:
sinfo            # idle is free, mix is partly used, alloc is full
squeue           # what is running and queued

The live cluster status dashboard gives the same view of free GPUs, queue depth, and contention.

docs.title: My job is stuck in PD (pending). What does that mean?
docs.text:
Pending is normal. Run squeue --me and read the reason in parentheses.

  • Resources means the GPUs you asked for are busy, and you are next in line when they free up.
  • Priority means other jobs are ahead of you in the queue.
  • QOSMaxWallDurationPerJobLimit means you asked for more time than allowed. Resubmit with a shorter --time.

squeue --me --start shows an estimated start time.

docs.title: Can I submit a job and come back later?
docs.text: From July 1, yes. Batch submission with sbatch needs every home directory on the shared storage, so it switches on when soft enforcement begins, once the June 30 migration is complete. Until then, use salloc for everything. For a long run, hold the allocation in tmux so it survives a sleeping laptop or a dropped connection: run salloc, then ssh <node> from inside the tmux session, detach with Ctrl-b d, and reattach later with tmux attach.

docs.title: Can I still use VS Code Remote-SSH?
docs.text: Yes. Allocate a node with salloc, then point VS Code Remote-SSH at that node. See the VS Code page.

docs.title: My time limit is too short for my training run.
docs.text:
You have three options.

  1. Ask for more time up front, for example --time=24:00:00, up to three days in main.
  2. Submit the run as a batch job with sbatch so it runs unattended.
  3. Add checkpointing to your code so a job can resume where it left off. The sysadmin team is happy to help you set this up.

docs.title: I have a paper or demo deadline. Can I get priority?
docs.text: Yes. Ask in #server and the sysadmin team can raise your queue priority for a set window so your jobs start sooner. This is a normal, supported part of how the cluster runs.

docs.title: Does any of this change my login, files, or environment?
docs.text: No. You keep the same username and password, the same conda environments, containers, and tools, and the same home directory path and contents. Your home now lives on shared storage, which is why you need to migrate your data off the old per-node disks by June 30. The only new step is requesting resources before you use a node, whether a GPU or just cores and memory.

docs.title: Where did my GPU go when my allocation ended?
docs.text: It returned to the shared pool for the next person. Returning resources when your time is up is what keeps a free GPU available when you need one, rather than reserved and idle by someone who has walked away.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Ask in #server. No question is too basic.

docs.title: Running jobs
docs.text: You work from the login node, which you reach with ssh <you>@sprlab005.csl.illinois.edu. From there you request an allocation from SLURM and then connect to the compute node it assigns you. This page covers the common cases, and the Command reference lists every command in brief.

docs.title: Request a GPU
docs.text:
salloc reserves resources and gives you an interactive allocation. Ask for the number of GPUs and the wall-clock time you need:

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00     # one GPU for four hours
salloc --gres=gpu:2 --time=2:00:00     # both GPUs on a node, for two hours

Each node has two GPUs, so two is the most you can request on a single node. After the allocation is granted, squeue --me shows which node you received.

docs.title: Request CPUs only
docs.text:
Work that does not use a GPU goes through SLURM in the same way. Request cores and memory and leave off --gres:

salloc --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=4:00:00

A job that requests a GPU receives a generous default share of cores and memory automatically, so you only need --cpus-per-task and --mem when you want something different from the default.

docs.title: Connect to your node
docs.text:
Once you hold an allocation, connect to the assigned node and work normally:

ssh <node>        # for example, sprc01
nvidia-smi        # the GPUs available to you

Your SSH session joins the allocation and is bound by the same limits, so your editors, conda environments, and containers all behave as they do today.

docs.title: Time limits
docs.text: Every allocation has a wall-clock limit set by --time in HH:MM:SS form. When the time runs out, the allocation ends and the resources return to the pool. The main partition allows up to three days for a single job. Set --time to what you realistically need, and request more on your next run if you come up short. If a job ends before you expected, run sacct -j <jobid> and read the State column; TIMEOUT means the job reached its limit.

docs.title: Long runs
docs.text:
For a long interactive session, start tmux on the login node before you allocate, so the session survives a dropped connection or a sleeping laptop:

tmux                                    # start tmux on the login node
salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=24:00:00     # hold the allocation
ssh <node>                              # work on the node

Detach from tmux with Ctrl-b then d, and reattach later with tmux attach.

docs.title: Batch jobs
docs.text:
From July 1, sbatch lets you submit a job and walk away. SLURM runs it when resources are free and writes its output to a file. Put your resource requests at the top of the script as #SBATCH lines:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --job-name=train
srun python train.py

Submit it with sbatch train.sh and follow its progress with squeue --me. Until soft enforcement begins on July 1, use salloc inside tmux for long runs.

docs.title: Deadlines
docs.text:
When you have a paper or demo deadline, the sysadmin team can raise your queue priority for a set window. Ask in #server. Once your account holds the expedite priority, add --qos=expedite to your request:

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=8:00:00 --qos=expedite

docs.title: During the optional period
docs.text: Until soft enforcement begins on July 1, GPU isolation is not yet active, so nvidia-smi on a node lists all of its GPUs rather than only the ones you reserved. Please use only the GPUs your allocation granted you. Check the dashboard or squeue to see what is already running on a node so that you do not overlap with someone else. From July 1 onward, an allocation sees only the GPUs it reserved.

docs.title: About the transition
docs.text:
This page explains why the cluster is moving to SLURM, what changes for you, and when each stage takes effect.

First, migrate your data by Tuesday, June 30

Before anything else, the per-node home directories and the /mnt/data1 data drive on the compute nodes are erased after June 30. Move your work to the shared storage now. See Migrate your data.

docs.title: Why the cluster is changing
docs.text:
The sprc cluster has four machines and eight high-end GPUs shared across the whole lab. Until now, nothing managed who used what, which led to three recurring problems.

  1. GPUs held but not used. Someone starts a process, then leaves, and the GPU stays reserved and idle while others wait for it.
  2. No fairness. Someone who has already used the cluster heavily this week has the same chance at the next free GPU as someone who has not touched it.
  3. No visibility. Because nothing recorded usage, the lab could not answer basic questions such as how busy the cluster really is, or whether it needs more hardware.

SLURM addresses all three. It is the scheduler used by most university HPC clusters, so it is well understood and well supported.

docs.title: What changes for you
docs.text:
The one real change is that you request the resources you need before you use a compute node:

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00              # a GPU
salloc --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=4:00:00   # CPU cores and memory, no GPU

Everything else stays the same. You keep your login and password, your home directory and files (once they are on the shared storage), your code, conda environments, and containers, and your editors and tools, including VS Code Remote-SSH and tmux.

Two habits are new. The first is time limits: a four-hour request ends after four hours, so for longer work you ask for more time up front and hold the allocation in tmux so it survives a disconnect. The second is that resources return to the pool when your time is up, which is what makes a free GPU available when you need one.

This applies to all compute-node work. CPU-only jobs go through SLURM the same way GPU jobs do, with the same allocations, time limits, and fair-share scheduling. The only GPU-specific piece is GPU isolation, which simply has nothing to apply to a job that requested no GPU.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text:
The dates are fixed through soft enforcement. Hard enforcement follows later, on a date announced ahead of time.

Stage When What you notice Optional period and data migration now to June 30 SLURM is live to try with salloc, and your direct-SSH workflow still works. Move your data to the shared storage before June 30. See Migrate your data. Data wipe after June 30 The per-node home directories and /mnt/data1 drives are erased. Soft enforcement July 1 Work inside an allocation gains time limits, fair-share scheduling, and GPU isolation, and sbatch becomes available. Direct SSH still works, so try the new workflow and report any issues. Hard enforcement to be announced An allocation is required to use a compute node. Direct SSH without one is declined, with sysadmin accounts excepted.

docs.title: What soft enforcement means
docs.text:
From July 1, work you run inside an allocation is bounded. If you use salloc or sbatch, the job receives time limits and fair-share scheduling, where queue order reflects recent usage, and a GPU job also receives GPU isolation, so it sees only the GPUs it reserved. CPU-only jobs receive the time limits and fair-share scheduling as well.

Batch submission with sbatch becomes available on July 1, once every home directory is on the shared storage.

Direct SSH still works during this period. You can connect to a compute node as before, with or without an allocation, since nothing is blocked yet. Use the optional period to try the allocation-based workflow and report any issues so the sysadmin team can resolve them before hard enforcement.

docs.title: Deadlines are protected
docs.text: Fair scheduling does not override real deadlines. If you have a paper or demo, ask in #server and the sysadmin team can raise your queue priority for a set window so your jobs start sooner. There is a supported priority path that the sysadmins control.

docs.title: Try it now
docs.text:
The best way to be ready is to use SLURM during the optional period, while your old workflow is still available:

salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00     # request a GPU, then ssh to your node
squeue --me                            # your jobs
sinfo                                  # what is free

See the Command reference for the full set of commands, and the FAQ for common questions.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Ask in #server. If you are unsure how to move your specific workflow onto SLURM, describe it in the channel and the sysadmin team will help.

docs.title: Migrate your data
docs.text:
Migrate your data by Tuesday, June 30

Your sprc home directories and the /mnt/data1 data drive on the compute nodes (sprc00 through sprc03) are erased after June 30, ahead of soft enforcement on July 1. Copy anything you want to keep to the shared storage before then, and mark your name in the migration sheet linked in the #server announcement.

docs.title: What is happening
docs.text:
The cluster now has shared storage that every node sees at the same place. Your home directory on the login node, sprlab005, already lives there. What is going away is the per-node local storage on the compute nodes:

  • the local home directories on sprc00 through sprc03, and
  • the /mnt/data1 data drive on those nodes.

These are erased after June 30 so the cluster can run on a single shared home for soft enforcement. Anything you have only on a compute node's local disk is lost unless you copy it to the shared storage first.

docs.title: What you need to do
docs.text:
1. Find your shared home directory. It is the same directory everywhere, mounted at two paths:

  • On the compute nodes (sprc00 through sprc03): /mnt/spr_storage/home/<your-username>
  • On the login node (sprlab005): /home/<your-username>, which is already shared storage, so anything already here is safe.

2. Copy your work into it. Log in to each compute node where you have data, and copy your local home and your /mnt/data1 work onto the shared home. For example, on a compute node, with <you> replaced by your username:

# local home  ->  shared home
rsync -aAXH --info=progress2 /home/<you>/      /mnt/spr_storage/home/<you>/

# data drive  ->  a folder in your shared home
rsync -aAXH --info=progress2 /mnt/data1/<you>/ /mnt/spr_storage/home/<you>/data1/

Adjust the source paths to wherever your data actually lives. rsync is restartable, so if it is interrupted, run the same command again and it continues where it left off.

3. Check that it landed:

ls -la /mnt/spr_storage/home/<you>/
du -sh /mnt/spr_storage/home/<you>/

4. Mark your name in the migration sheet linked in the #server announcement, so the sysadmin team can confirm your data has moved.

docs.title: Quota
docs.text: Shared storage has a 50 GB quota per user. Check your usage with du -sh /mnt/spr_storage/home/<you>/. If your data is larger than 50 GB, post in #server before you copy and the sysadmin team will raise your quota, otherwise the copy stops when you reach the limit.

docs.title: After June 30
docs.text:
• The per-node home directories and /mnt/data1 drives are erased.
  • Soft enforcement begins on July 1. Work you run inside an allocation gains time limits and fair-share scheduling, GPU jobs gain GPU isolation, and sbatch becomes available. Direct SSH still works. See About the transition.

docs.title: Help
docs.text: If you are unsure what to keep, or you are concerned about the quota, ask in #server before the deadline and the sysadmin team will help you sort it out.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text: VS Code Remote-SSH continues to work. The one change is that you connect to a compute node only after you hold an allocation on it, whether that allocation is for a GPU or for CPU cores and memory.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
1. Log in to the login node and request a node.

    ssh <you>@sprlab005.csl.illinois.edu
salloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=4:00:00

    salloc prints the node you were granted, for example sprc01. Keep this terminal open. Closing it, or letting the time run out, releases the node.

  2. Point VS Code at that node. Open the Remote Explorer, or run Remote-SSH: Connect to Host, and connect to the node name (for example, sprc01).

  3. Work normally. Open your folder, edit, run cells, and use the integrated terminal. During the optional period, nvidia-smi in the VS Code terminal lists all of the node's GPUs, so use only the ones you reserved.

  4. When you finish, close VS Code and run exit in the salloc terminal, or let the time expire, to return the node to the pool.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Allocate first, then connect. Connecting VS Code to a node where you hold no allocation still works through soft enforcement on July 1, but at hard enforcement that connection is declined. Build the habit now: salloc, then connect. From July 1, an allocation sees only the GPUs it reserved.
  • Keep the salloc terminal alive. That terminal holds your allocation. If it closes, the node is released and your VS Code session loses access.
  • Reuse one allocation. You do not need a fresh allocation for each VS Code window. While the salloc is live, open as many VS Code or SSH sessions to that node as you like.
  • Long runs do not need VS Code. For multi-hour training, start the run inside tmux on the allocated node so it survives a sleeping laptop or a dropped connection, and reattach later with tmux attach. Use VS Code Remote-SSH for interactive development and debugging.

docs.title: Help
docs.text: If you have trouble connecting, ask in #server and the sysadmin team will help you sort out your SSH configuration.

docs.title: Sysadmin reference
docs.text: These pages are internal runbooks for the sysadmin team. They are kept here in the open so that anyone curious about how the cluster is administered can read them, but they are not part of the day-to-day workflow for cluster users. If you are looking for how to run jobs, start at Running jobs.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: • New user provisioning: steps to set a new user's storage quota.

docs.title: New user provisioning
docs.text:
When provisioning a new user, set their ZFS dataset quota on sprlab005. The loop below applies the standard 50 GB per-user quota to every home account (UID 1000 and above) on the spr-storage/home dataset:

for uid in $(getent passwd | awk -F: '$6 ~ /^\/home\// && $3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $3}'); do
  sudo zfs set userquota@${uid}=50G spr-storage/home
done

Run this from the admin account with sudo. To raise a single user's quota, set userquota@<uid> to the agreed value rather than the 50 GB default.
